summary_grc: ὁ Εὔδημος δικαστής ἐστι καὶ μισθὸν λαμβάνει· ὁ δὲ Δημόκριτος καὶ ὁ Ἀρίστων περὶ τοῦ μισθοῦ διαλέγονται.
summary_en: Eudemos, a refugee with no fields to work, sits as a juror for two obols a day. Demokritos complains that pay has handed the courts to the poor; Ariston defends it. Why did Pericles bring in pay? Aristotle's answer, adapted: to match the private generosity of the rich Cimon.
caption_grc: ἡ πόλις τοῖς δικασταῖς μισθὸν δίδωσιν, δύο ὀβολοὺς τῆς ἡμέρας.

original.note: Aristotle (or a pupil), Constitution of the Athenians 27.3, which paragraph 3 adapts; written about 330 BC. Jury pay was introduced by Pericles around 450; it was two obols a day in our story (431) and three from about 425. The next section (27.4) adds that some blamed pay for making the courts worse, since ordinary men rather than respectable ones put themselves forward for the lot. This lesson takes the place of the 'Old Oligarch' (pseudo-Xenophon, Constitution of the Athenians 1.1–2), which argues the same question from the other side but is not in the Perseus corpus the course draws on.

grammar.md:
**The language of the democracy.** Athenian laws and decrees, and writers about them, use a handful of set phrases. Learn to see them as blocks.

**ὁ βουλόμενος 'anyone who wishes'.** The article with a present participle makes a noun: ὁ βουλόμενος is 'the one who wishes', i.e. *any citizen who wants to*. It is how Athenian law opened a prosecution or a debate to everyone: τῷ βουλομένῳ ἐξῆν … 'it was open to anyone who wished …'. In the Assembly the herald asked τίς ἀγορεύειν βούλεται; 'who wishes to speak?'.

**Impersonal ἔξεστι 'it is allowed, possible'.** It takes a dative of the person and an infinitive:

| form | example |
|---|---|
| ἔξεστι (present) | ἔξεστι τοῖς πένησι δικάζειν |
| ἐξῆν (imperfect) | ἐξῆν τῷ βουλομένῳ … ἔχειν τὰ μέτρια |
| ἐξῇ (subjunctive) | ὅπως ἐξῇ τῷ βουλομένῳ … ἀπολαύειν |
| ἐξέσται (future) | ἐξέσται σοι λέγειν |

**ἅτε + participle: the author's reason.** ὁ Κίμων, ἅτε τυραννικὴν ἔχων οὐσίαν … 'Cimon, since he had a fortune fit for a tyrant …'. ἅτε marks a cause the writer vouches for; ὡς + participle (Unit 9) gives a reason someone else alleges.

**The imperfect of habit.** ἔτρεφε πολλούς 'he used to feed many', ἐποίει τὰς λειτουργίας 'he regularly paid for public services': continuous or repeated action in the past.

**Rich and poor.** πλούσιος, -α, -ον 'rich' ↔ ὁ πένης, τοῦ πένητος 'poor man' (3rd declension; dative plural πένησι(ν), with the τ lost before σ). A πένης works for his living; a beggar is πτωχός.

culture.title: Paying citizens to take part
culture.md:
Athens paid its citizens to govern. From about 450 BC a juror received **two obols** for each day's sitting (three from about 425, on Cleon's proposal); a councillor received five obols in the fourth century; and from the 390s, after attendance fell, citizens were paid for going to the **Assembly** too: first one obol, then two, then three, and later a drachma or more. An unskilled labourer earned about a drachma (six obols) a day, so jury pay was a modest living, most welcome to the old and to men without work, like the Acharnian refugees crowded into the city in 431.

The critics of democracy hated it. Plato's Socrates says that Pericles 'made the Athenians idle, cowardly, talkative and greedy' by introducing pay (*Gorgias* 515e); Aristophanes' *Wasps* (422) mocks old jurors who live for the three obols they carry home in their mouths. Its defenders saw the point plainly: without pay, only the rich could afford to sit in the courts and the Council, and the rule of the people would become the rule of the few. The picture shows a bronze juror's ticket (πινάκιον) with its owner's name and deme, from the fourth century.
